title: The Sign of Immanuel
sum: About 734 BC Aram and Israel march on Jerusalem to force Judah into their revolt against Assyria. The LORD sends Isaiah, with his son Shear-jashub ("a remnant will return"), to meet King Ahaz at the water channel where he is checking the city's water supply. The message is short: stay calm; these two kings are smoking stubs; their plan will not stand. Then the warning, in a play on one Hebrew root: "If you will not hold firm, you will not be held firm" (7:9).

Ahaz refuses to ask for a sign, with pious words that hide a decision already made: he will buy help from Assyria. Isaiah gives a sign anyway. A young woman is pregnant and will name her son Immanuel, "God is with us", and before the boy is old enough to choose, the two enemy kingdoms will be empty. But the same Assyria Ahaz is courting will strip Judah bare, and the chapter ends with four "On that day" pictures of a land shaved, emptied and overgrown.
readings: Read as history

The chapter is a report from a real crisis, told alongside 2 Kings 16. Isaiah offers Ahaz a political choice framed as faith: trust the LORD's promise to David's house, or become Assyria's vassal. The sign is a child born in those months, and the time-limit came true when Damascus fell in 732 BC. On this reading, 7:14 is first of all a word to Ahaz.
Read as prophecy of Christ

Matthew 1:22–23 reads the sign as fulfilled in Jesus' birth from the virgin Mary, and most Christians through the centuries have read 7:14 that way, some as a direct prediction only, others as a sign to Ahaz whose full meaning arrived with Jesus. The name Immanuel and the royal child of 9:6–7 and 11:1–5 point beyond any child of Ahaz's day.
Read as part of a book

Chapters 6–8 are framed as Isaiah's own memoir, with his children as living signs (8:18). Chapter 7 contrasts Ahaz, who will not trust, with Hezekiah in chapters 36–37, who meets the Assyrian envoy at the very same channel (36:2) and does trust. The book sets the two kings side by side on purpose.

views.H: In 734–732 BC Tiglath-pileser III swept through the west; Ahaz paid him tribute (2 Kings 16:7–9), and Assyria took Damascus, killed Rezin and stripped Israel of Galilee and Gilead. Tiglath-pileser's own inscriptions list "Jehoahaz of Judah", that is, Ahaz, among the kings who paid. The time-sign of 7:16 came true within about three years. The 65 years of 7:8 are harder: the settling of foreigners in Samaria under Esarhaddon, about 670 BC, is the usual explanation.
views.C: Most critical scholars take 6:1–9:6 as an early collection, the "Isaiah memoir", built around the prophet's children. Chapter 7 is told in the third person, unlike 6 and 8, which suggests a disciple's hand. Many think 7:8b (the 65 years) and the "On that day" sayings of 7:18–25 were added later. The sign is usually read as a child of Isaiah's own day, perhaps a royal heir, with the hope of 9:1–7 and 11:1–9 growing from it.
views.J: Jewish interpreters read the sign within Ahaz's lifetime. Trypho in Justin's Dialogue already names Hezekiah; Rashi and Ibn Ezra take the young woman as Isaiah's wife and the child as his son, since 8:3–4 repeats the time-sign; Radak and others suggest Ahaz's young wife. Jewish polemic since the Middle Ages, in the Nizzahon Vetus (13th century) and Isaac of Troki's Chizzuk Emunah (about 1594), has used 7:14 as a test case for Christian reading of the prophets, stressing that 'almah does not mean "virgin" and that the sign was for Ahaz.
views.X: The church read 7:14 as a prophecy of the virgin birth from the 2nd century on (Justin, Irenaeus), in the wording of the Greek, "the virgin". Some read it as direct prediction (Calvin, E. J. Young); many modern Christian scholars see a sign for Ahaz whose fuller meaning Matthew discerned in Jesus. Immanuel, "God is with us", frames Matthew's Gospel, which ends with Jesus' promise to be with his disciples (Matthew 28:20).
views.F: Readers who look for future fulfillment mostly treat chapter 7 as fulfilled: in Ahaz's day and in Jesus' birth. They find its future dimension in the Immanuel figure of 8:8 and 9:6–7, whose throne and endless peace they place at Christ's return.

deep.h: The witnesses read for these chapters
deep.b: The Plain of Isaiah 7–12 follows the Masoretic Text of the Leningrad Codex, with its Ketiv and Qere. The Dead Sea Scrolls were read directly for every verse, in the ETCBC transcription: the complete Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC), 1QIsa-b (1Q8) and the fragments 4QIsa-a to -r (4Q55–4Q69) where they cover these chapters. The Greek was read in Swete's edition, which prints Codex Vaticanus; where the note says "the Greek", it means that text, checked against Ziegler's critical edition as reported in the commentaries. The Targum is cited as reported in Bruce Chilton's translation, and the Vulgate from Weber's edition. Readings of Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion are given only as reported by ancient writers.

deep.h: Isaiah 7:14: the sign, the young woman and Matthew
deep.b:
The sign is offered to "the house of David" (7:13), and "you" in 7:14 is plural: the whole royal house, not Ahaz alone. Three facts shape every reading. The word. 'Almah is a young woman of marriageable age; it does not in itself state virginity, and the usual word for that is betulah. Yet no text uses 'almah of a married woman, and the Greek translators chose parthenos. The time. The sign is tied to Ahaz's crisis: before the boy can choose good from bad, Aram and Israel will be abandoned (7:16). The name. Immanuel returns as the owner of the land (8:8) and as a cry of faith (8:10), and the child of 9:6–7 seems to fill out the same hope.

From these come the main readings. A child of Ahaz's day only: Hezekiah, Isaiah's son, or any child named in hope (Jewish interpreters and many critical scholars). A direct prophecy of Jesus only: the virgin is Mary, and the time-sign in 7:16 refers to a different child or is a measure of time (Calvin; Edward J. Young; many evangelicals). A double or typological fulfillment: a birth in Ahaz's day was the first sign, and Matthew saw the full meaning in Jesus, conceived without a human father (many Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant scholars). Most modern translations, Jewish and Christian, and many evangelical study notes discuss the same question, and most put "young woman" in the text or the margin. Each reading answers a real feature of the text, and none needs to be held in bad faith.

Matthew quotes the Greek, "the virgin will be pregnant", and adds the meaning of the name (Matthew 1:23). Justin Martyr's Dialogue with Trypho (about AD 155) records the debate already in full: Trypho argues for neanis, "young woman", and Hezekiah; Justin for parthenos and Christ. See the notes and the variants at 7:14.

echoes: 2 Kings 16:1–20; 2 Chronicles 28:1–27; 2 Kings 18:17; 36:2; 2 Chronicles 20:20; Genesis 16:11; Judges 13:3–5; Genesis 24:43; Exodus 2:8; Proverbs 30:19; Matthew 1:23; Luke 1:31; 8:3–4; 8:8; 9:6–7

settings.what: Isaiah meets Ahaz at the water channel
settings.by: The LORD, through Isaiah, with his son Shear-jashub beside him
settings.to: King Ahaz and his court, inspecting Jerusalem's water supply before a siege
settings.when: About 734 BC, as Aram and Israel march on Jerusalem to replace Ahaz with "the son of Tabeal"
settings.why: The words are meant to calm a panicking king and to call him to trust the LORD's promise to David's house instead of appealing to Assyria. The boy's name, "a remnant will return", is itself a message: judgment and survival together. Knowing that Ahaz had already decided to send tribute to Assyria (2 Kings 16:7) shows what "hold firm" means here: rely on God, not on a foreign army.
settings.readers: For later readers, the scene is set beside Hezekiah's at the same spot (36:2): two kings of David's line, one who would not trust and one who did.

settings.to: Ahaz, and through him "the house of David" (the plural "you")
settings.when: Soon after the first meeting, while the threat still stands
settings.why: Ahaz's refusal to ask for a sign uses the law's words (Deuteronomy 6:16) to cover unbelief. The sign that follows works both ways: a child named "God is with us" means the enemy kingdoms will fall quickly, but it also means the LORD is present to judge a royal house that will not trust him, and Assyria will come. The sign is good news and a rebuke at once.
views: The child is born in those months, and the sign is the short time before the threat ends (most critical and Jewish readers).
A sign of the far future
The sign is the virgin birth of the Messiah, which assures the house of David that it will not be destroyed (Calvin, E. J. Young).
A child of that day was the first sign; Jesus is its final fulfillment (many Christian scholars).

settings.when: Probably gathered after the 734 BC crisis; some think they were added later
settings.why: The short sayings spell out what Assyria will do to Judah: swarm in like flies and bees, shave it like a captive, leave a few survivors living on curds and honey, and turn prime vineyards into thornbush. They answer Ahaz's policy: the empire he hired as a rescuer will be the razor in the LORD's hand.

title: Fear the LORD Alone
sum: Isaiah writes a strange name on a large tablet before witnesses: Maher-shalal-hash-baz, "quick to the plunder, swift to the spoil". Then his wife, "the prophetess", bears a son with that name, and before the baby can say "Daddy" or "Mommy", Damascus and Samaria will be plundered by Assyria. Because the people despise the gentle waters of Shiloah, the LORD will bring the flood of the Euphrates, Assyria itself, up to Judah's neck. Yet the nations' plans will fail, "for God is with us".

The second half is private. The LORD grips Isaiah and warns him not to share the people's panic. The LORD alone is to be feared: he is a holy refuge and a stone that trips both houses of Israel. Isaiah seals his teaching among his disciples and waits for the LORD, who is hiding his face, while he and his children stand as signs. Those who turn to the ghosts of the dead instead will find only darkness.
readings: Read as history

The chapter tracks the same crisis as chapter 7. Assyria did plunder Damascus (732 BC) and Samaria (722 BC) and did flood Judah in 701 BC, reaching "up to the neck" when only Jerusalem was left (2 Kings 18:13). Isaiah's withdrawal to his disciples is a prophet rejected by his king.
Read as the birth of a community

In 8:11–22 Isaiah and his disciples become a small group who trust the LORD against the majority. The sealed teaching waits for a later day. Many see here the origin of the circle that preserved and continued Isaiah's words.
Read in the New Testament

The chapter is quoted more than its length suggests: the stone of stumbling (Romans 9:33; 1 Peter 2:8), "do not fear what they fear" (1 Peter 3:14–15), and "I will trust in him ... I and the children God has given me" (Hebrews 2:13), each applied to Jesus and his followers.

views.H: Tiglath-pileser took Damascus in 732 BC and much of Israel's territory; Samaria fell to Shalmaneser V and Sargon II in 722. Sennacherib's invasion of 701 BC took 46 of Judah's walled towns, by his own account, and left Jerusalem alone. The Shiloah channel ran along the eastern hill from the Gihon spring, before Hezekiah's tunnel replaced it.
views.C: The first-person narrative (8:1–18) continues the Isaiah memoir. Many scholars see 8:19–22 as a later addition that links the memoir to 9:1–7. The flood picture (8:7–8) is close to Assyrian royal language, which describes the king's army as a flood. The words "Immanuel" in 8:8 and 8:10 tie the oracles to the sign of 7:14.
views.J: Rabbinic tradition identifies the witness Zechariah son of Jeberechiah with a later prophet and reads 8:2 with Zechariah 8:4: as Uriah's prophecy of ruin came true, so will Zechariah's of rebuilding (Makkot 24b). Rashi takes the prophetess as Isaiah's wife. 8:19–20 is a classic text against consulting the dead.
views.X: The New Testament reads 8:14 with 28:16 of Christ as the stone that some stumble on and others build on, and Hebrews 2:13 puts 8:17–18 in Jesus' mouth. Christian readers have heard in 8:10 the same promise as Immanuel, and have taken 8:16–20 as a model for the faithful few under pressure.
views.F: Some read 8:9–10, the nations that rage and are broken, alongside Psalm 2 and Revelation 19 as a picture of a final assault on God's people that fails.

deep.b:
Isaiah's household is a message in itself. His name means "the LORD saves"; his sons are Shear-jashub, "a remnant will return" (7:3), and Maher-shalal-hash-baz, "quick to the plunder" (8:3); and Immanuel, "God is with us" (7:14), may be a third child or a royal one. "Look at me and the children the LORD has given me: we are signs and omens in Israel" (8:18). Each name compresses a part of Isaiah's preaching: salvation, judgment, a surviving remnant, and God's presence. The book later uses the same names as themes: the remnant returns in 10:20–22, Assyria plunders in 10:6, and God is with his people in the song of chapter 12.

Hebrews 2:13 quotes the Greek of 8:17–18 as words of Christ, who stands with "the children God has given" him and shares their flesh and blood. Isaiah's small circle of children and disciples becomes, in that reading, a picture of the church gathered around Jesus.

echoes: 7:14; 28:16; 2 Kings 16:10–16; 2 Kings 18:13; Psalm 46:4–7; Romans 9:33; 1 Peter 2:8; 1 Peter 3:14–15; Hebrews 2:13; Matthew 4:12–16; Leviticus 19:31; Deuteronomy 18:10–12; 1 Samuel 28:7–19

settings.by: Isaiah, telling what the LORD told him to do
settings.to: The people of Jerusalem, who could read the public tablet; the two named witnesses
settings.when: During the 734 BC crisis, about nine months or more before the child's birth
settings.why: Writing the name in public, with reliable witnesses, before the child was conceived, made the prophecy checkable: when Damascus and Samaria fell within a year or two, everyone could see the LORD had said so beforehand. The act gives the people a second sign beside Immanuel, with the same short clock.

settings.what: The waters of Shiloah and the River
settings.to: "This people": Judah, and perhaps those in Judah who welcomed the coalition
settings.when: During or soon after the crisis
settings.why: The gentle channel stands for the LORD's quiet care for Jerusalem; the Euphrates stands for Assyria. Those who scorn the one will drown in the other. "Takes joy in Rezin" may mean a party in Judah favored the coalition, or the people's delight when the enemy kings fell. The oracle ends on a turn: the land still belongs to Immanuel.
views: The people of Judah are rebuked for not trusting the LORD's care (most readers).
The words were first against Israel, which joined Rezin, and were later applied to Judah (some critics).

settings.by: Isaiah, or the people of Zion in a song of faith
settings.to: The nations, addressed in poetry; heard by Judah
settings.when: Uncertain: in the crisis, or later
settings.why: After the flood comes defiance: the nations can arm and plot, but they will be broken, because God is with his people. The words turn the name Immanuel into a confession that steadies the hearers.

settings.what: The LORD's private word to Isaiah
settings.to: Isaiah and the small group around him (the verbs are plural)
settings.when: As the city panics over plots and alliances
settings.why: The word sets the prophet's circle apart from the crowd: do not see conspiracies everywhere or fear what they fear; fear the LORD. He will be a sanctuary for those who trust and a stone that trips the rest. It gives a faithful minority a way to stand when leaders and people go the other way.

settings.to: His disciples (8:16, 19), warned against those who urge them to consult the dead
settings.when: After Ahaz has rejected his message
settings.why: Isaiah entrusts his teaching to his followers, to be kept until events prove it, and waits for the LORD. He warns those who turn to mediums that they will see no dawn. The passage explains how a rejected prophet's words survived: they were written, sealed and handed on.
settings.readers: For later generations, perhaps in exile, the sealed teaching was the book they now held, and the dark of 8:22 the darkness that 9:2 says will end.

title: A Child Has Been Born to Us
sum: Darkness turns to light. Galilee, the first region Assyria stripped from Israel, will be the first to see a great light. The oppressor's yoke is broken as on the day Gideon beat Midian, the boots and bloody cloaks of war are burned, and the reason is a child: a son given to rule on David's throne, named Wonder-Counselor, Mighty God, Father Forever, Prince of Peace. His peace will have no end, and "the zeal of the LORD of Armies will make it happen" (9:7).

The second half is a poem of judgment on the northern kingdom, with a refrain at the end of each stanza: "In spite of all this, his anger has not turned back, / and his hand is still stretched out" (9:12, 17, 21; 10:4). Israel shrugs off disaster with a boast, its leaders mislead, wickedness burns like a brush fire, and the tribes devour each other.
readings: Read as a royal hymn

Many scholars read 9:2–7 as a song for the birth or crowning of a king of Judah, with throne names like those given to Egyptian kings. The king in view is often taken to be Hezekiah. The hope it voices is that David's line will bring the justice and peace promised in 2 Samuel 7.
Read as prophecy of the Messiah

The Targum names the child the Messiah, and the church has always read the verse of Jesus, the son "given" by God. The names, above all "Mighty God" (also used of the LORD in 10:21), and a rule with "no end" go beyond any king of Judah.
Read as two halves of one message

The light of 9:1–7 and the dark refrain of 9:8–10:4 belong together. The book sets the promised king between the sealed teaching of chapter 8 and the judgment on Ephraim, so that hope is never cheap: it comes through judgment, not around it.

views.H: In 733–732 BC Tiglath-pileser annexed Galilee, the coastal plain and Gilead and deported many of their people (2 Kings 15:29). Those are the regions of 9:1. Scholars reconstruct three Assyrian provinces there. The hope was that this first-humbled land would be the first restored. The judgment poem matches the north's last decades: Aram and the Philistines attacking (9:12), civil wars and royal murders (2 Kings 15), until Samaria fell in 722 BC.
views.C: Many date 9:2–7 to Isaiah himself, as an accession oracle for Hezekiah (about 715 BC) or for an expected heir; others to a later king such as Josiah, or after the exile. The refrain poem of 9:8–10:4 has been split from a stanza now in 5:25–30, which may once have ended it. The closed mem in 9:7 (Hebrew 9:6) is a scribal oddity with many explanations.
views.J: The Targum makes the child the Messiah, adding "in whose days peace will increase". Rashi and other medieval commentators read the child as Hezekiah and take the first names as names of God: God, the Wonder-Counselor, the Mighty God, the Father Forever, calls the child "Prince of Peace". The Talmud says God wished to make Hezekiah the Messiah, and reads the closed mem as a sign that the hope was closed for a time (Sanhedrin 94a). The New JPS translation renders the names as one sentence about God.
views.X: Matthew 4:13–16 applies 9:1–2 to Jesus' ministry in Galilee, and Luke 1:32–33 echoes 9:7: the son of the Most High will receive David's throne and his kingdom will have no end. The church read "Mighty God" of Christ's divinity. Handel set 9:2 and 9:6 in Messiah, and 9:2–7 is read at Christmas in many churches.
views.F: Many futurist readers place the full peace of 9:7, with no end, on David's throne, at Christ's reign on earth after his return, while the light of 9:2 began with his first coming.

deep.b:
The Hebrew has four pairs of words: pele' yo'ets, 'el gibbor, 'avi'ad, sar shalom. Names of the king. Most Christian readers, and many critical scholars, take them as the child's throne names, like the five-part titles given to Egyptian kings at their crowning: a counselor whose plans are a wonder, a mighty God (or "godlike hero"), a father to his people forever, a ruler who brings peace. Names that praise God. Israelite names often were sentences about God (Isaiah means "the LORD saves"). Rashi read the first three as God, who names the child "Prince of Peace"; the New JPS translation makes the whole a single name about God's purpose of peace. One name in Greek. The Greek has only "Angel (messenger) of great counsel". The Targum keeps four, adds "Messiah", and makes the child's days days of increasing peace.

"Mighty God" ('el gibbor) is the strongest point for those who see more than a human king: Isaiah uses the same words of the LORD in 10:21. Those who read a human king answer that royal language could be lofty (Psalm 45:6 addresses the king: "Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever") and that "godlike hero" is possible. For Christian readers the title fits the Son who is both David's heir and God. The note on 9:6 gives the details.

English Bibles begin chapter 9 one verse earlier than Hebrew Bibles: English 9:1 is Hebrew 8:23, and English 9:2–21 are Hebrew 9:1–20. This site uses the English numbers. In the Hebrew 9:6 (English 9:7), the word lemarbeh, "to the growth of", is written with the closed form of the letter mem, normally used only at the end of a word. The Great Isaiah Scroll writes it as two words, lm rbh, with an ordinary mem. The Masoretes kept the odd letter and noted it, and the Talmud (Sanhedrin 94a) explains it as a hint that the promise was closed in Hezekiah's day. Modern scholars think it began as a copying error, perhaps from a word divided as lahem rabbah, "to them great".

settings.what: The great light and the child-king
settings.by: Isaiah, speaking for a people who say "to us"
settings.to: Judah and the remnant of the north, after Galilee was lost to Assyria
settings.when: After 732 BC; perhaps at a royal birth or crowning
settings.why: The poem turns grief into praise before the fact. The regions first humbled will be first restored, the oppressor's yoke will break, and a king from David's line will rule with justice forever. For a people under Assyria, it shows that their hope rests on the LORD's zeal, not on alliances.
views: The child is Hezekiah or another heir, and the poem celebrates his birth or accession (many critical scholars; Rashi).
The child is the coming king of David's line (the Targum) or Jesus (the New Testament and the church).
The poem was written after the monarchy failed, for a king still to come (some critics).

settings.what: The poem of the outstretched hand
settings.to: The northern kingdom (Jacob, Israel, Ephraim, Samaria), heard in Judah; the last stanza (10:1–4) is aimed at the lawmakers and scribes who write unjust decrees
settings.when: In the years before Samaria fell in 722 BC
settings.why: Each stanza names a sin and a blow, and ends with the warning that the LORD's anger is not yet spent. The poem explains disaster as the LORD's discipline that Israel refused to learn from. Heard in Judah, it warned the southern kingdom not to repeat the north's pride and injustice; its last stanza (10:1–4) may already address Judah's officials.
settings.readers: For readers after 722 BC, the poem explained why the northern kingdom vanished.

title: The Rod of My Anger
sum: The outstretched-hand poem ends with a woe on officials who write unjust laws and loot widows and orphans. Then Isaiah turns to Assyria. The empire is the LORD's rod, sent against a godless nation, but its king thinks he has done it all himself and boasts that Jerusalem's God is no different from the idols of the cities he has crushed. Can an ax boast against the one who swings it? The LORD will burn the Assyrian's glory like a forest fire, leaving trees so few that a child could count them.

A remnant of Israel will return to the Mighty God, though only a remnant. Zion need not fear: the LORD will strike Assyria as he struck Midian and Egypt. The chapter ends with a breathless report of an enemy marching town by town to the hills north of Jerusalem, shaking his fist at Zion, and then the LORD felling him like a forest of Lebanon.
readings: Read as a theology of empire

Isaiah claims that the greatest power of his world is a tool in the LORD's hand, and that it will be judged for its pride and cruelty even while it serves him. The passage has shaped reflection on God's providence over nations ever since.
Read as history

The boasts of 10:8–11 echo the Assyrian kings' own inscriptions, listing cities they took in 740–717 BC. The march of 10:28–32 follows the road from the north to Nob, a day from Jerusalem, and matches the threat of 701 BC or an earlier campaign.
Read as hope for the remnant
The chapter's center, 10:20–23, takes up the name of Isaiah's son: a remnant will return. Paul reads it in Romans 9:27–28 as God keeping a remnant within Israel.

views.H: Tiglath-pileser III, Shalmaneser V, Sargon II and Sennacherib took the cities of 10:9: Arpad (740), Calno and Hamath (738; Hamath again in 720), Damascus (732), Samaria (722) and Carchemish (717). Sargon's and Sennacherib's inscriptions boast in language close to 10:13–14. In 701 BC Sennacherib's army withdrew from Jerusalem after a sudden disaster (37:36), which many see as the fulfillment of 10:16–19 and 10:33–34.
views.C: Most scholars hold that 10:5–15 is Isaiah's, from Sargon's or Sennacherib's reign, and that 10:16–27 contains later expansions. The march of 10:27–32 is variously dated: Sennacherib in 701, the coalition of 734 approaching from the north, or a stylized picture. Peter Machinist has shown how closely Isaiah's portrait of Assyria mirrors its own royal propaganda.
views.J: A famous midrash reads "Lebanon" in 10:34 as the Temple, which fell, and 11:1, which follows at once, as the Messiah, who was born on the day the Temple was destroyed (Lamentations Rabbah on 1:16). Rashi reads 10:33–34 of Sennacherib's army, destroyed outside Jerusalem. The Targum, as reported by Chilton, reads 10:27 as the nations being broken before the Messiah.
views.X: Paul quotes the Greek of 10:22–23 to argue that God has always saved a remnant (Romans 9:27–28). Christian thinkers from Augustine to Calvin used 10:5–15 to explain how God can use wicked rulers without approving their wickedness.
views.F: The Qumran commentaries applied 10:28–34 to the last war, and some later readers have done the same, reading the Assyrian as a figure of the final enemy who is destroyed before the Messiah reigns.

deep.h: An ax in the LORD's hand
deep.b: The center of chapter 10 is a puzzle that every theology of history faces. The LORD sends Assyria to punish "a godless nation" (10:6), but "he does not see it that way" (10:7): the Assyrian king means to wipe out nations, and boasts of his own strength and cleverness. Isaiah answers with a picture: an ax, a saw, a stick cannot take credit over the one who uses them (10:15). God's purpose and the human agent's purpose run side by side, and the agent is judged for his own intention. The same pattern returns with Babylon (47:6) and Cyrus (45:1–7), and in Joseph's words to his brothers: "You planned evil against me, but God planned it for good" (Genesis 50:20). Jewish and Christian readers have drawn very different lessons from it: comfort that no tyrant has the last word, and warning against claiming that any victory proves God is on one's side.

echoes: 5:8–25; Exodus 22:22–24; 37:21–38; 2 Kings 18:33–35; 2 Kings 19:23–28; Judges 7:25; Exodus 14:16; Genesis 22:17; Romans 9:27–28; 28:22; 1 Samuel 21:1; Jeremiah 1:1; Ezekiel 31:3–18

settings.what: Woe to the writers of unjust decrees
settings.to: The officials and scribes who write the laws, in Samaria or in Jerusalem
settings.when: The last stanza of the outstretched-hand poem (9:8–10:4), in the years before 722 BC
settings.why: The woe names a sin that law itself can commit: decrees that push the weak out of court and turn widows and orphans into loot. It asks the lawmakers where they will run on the day of accounting. Whether first aimed at the north or at Judah, it warned Jerusalem's officials that the north's fate could be theirs.
views: The stanza belongs to the poem against Ephraim and Samaria (many scholars).
The woe was first spoken against Judah's officials and joined to the poem later (others).

settings.to: Assyria, addressed in poetry; spoken to Judah
settings.when: Under Sargon II or Sennacherib, after Samaria's fall in 722 BC and probably before 701
settings.why: Assyria would never hear it, so the words are for Judah: the empire that terrifies you is the LORD's tool, and its boasting will be its downfall. They give Judah a reason not to bow to Assyria's gods or despair under its power.

settings.to: The survivors of Israel and Judah
settings.when: After the Assyrian disasters; many date it later
settings.why: The remnant name of 7:3 is unpacked: those who survive will stop relying on the empire that beat them and lean on the LORD. But it is only a remnant: the decreed end will still come. The words hold together comfort and sober warning.
The LORD's anger at his people will end soon and turn on the oppressor. Recalling Midian and the Red Sea, the oracle tells Jerusalem that the God who rescued Israel before will do it again.

settings.to: Jerusalem and the towns on the northern road
settings.when: During an invasion from the north: 701 BC, 734 BC, or a stylized picture
settings.why: The short, breathless lines make the hearers feel the danger coming closer town by town, until the enemy stands in sight of Zion. Then the LORD fells him like a forest. The poem teaches that the danger is real and that the LORD's rescue is sure.
views: The march pictures the Assyrian approach that ended at Jerusalem (many scholars).
The road from the north suits the coalition's march of chapter 7 (some scholars).
The route is a dramatic composition, not a report (others).

title: The Shoot from Jesse's Stump
sum: After the LORD fells Assyria's forest, a shoot grows from the stump of Jesse, David's father. The LORD's Spirit rests on this king with wisdom, counsel, strength, knowledge and the fear of the LORD. He judges the poor fairly, not by appearances; his word is his weapon; righteousness and faithfulness are his belt. Then the picture widens: wolf and lamb, leopard and goat, lion and calf live together, a small boy leads them, and a baby plays at a cobra's hole, because knowing the LORD fills the earth like the sea.

"On that day" the root of Jesse stands as a flag for the nations. The LORD reaches out a second time, as in the exodus, to gather the scattered of Israel and Judah from Assyria, Egypt and the ends of the earth. The old rivalry of north and south ends, the sea and the River are split, and a highway runs home for the remnant.
readings: Read as the Messiah's reign

Jewish and Christian tradition alike read 11:1–10 of the Messiah. For Jews it describes the king still to come and the peace of his days; for Christians it is Jesus, anointed with the Spirit, whose reign has begun and will be complete at his return.
Read as an ideal king

Many scholars read 11:1–5 as Isaiah's portrait of the just king Judah never had, after Ahaz's failure, and 11:6–9 as the peace that follows when the land is ruled by justice. The animals may be a poetic picture of a world without violence.
Read as new creation
The animals at peace recall Eden before bloodshed (Genesis 1:29–30) and look ahead to 65:17–25. On this reading the king's justice reaches into nature itself: creation is healed, not only society.

views.H: The chapter assumes David's line has been cut down to a stump. That suits the Assyrian period, when Judah was a vassal under Ahaz, or the exile, after 586 BC, when no king of David's house ruled. The list of 11:11 matches the lands where Israelites and Judeans lived after the Assyrian and Babylonian deportations, and the Jewish communities known in Egypt (Elephantine) and Babylonia.
views.C: Opinion is divided on 11:1–9: some hold it is Isaiah's, from Hezekiah's time; many date it after the fall of the monarchy, since it speaks of a stump. 11:10 is a link verse, and 11:11–16 is usually dated after the exile, with its second exodus like the hope of 40–55.
views.J: The Targum reads 11:1 of the Messiah from Jesse's sons, and the rabbis drew from 11:3 that the Messiah will judge by "smell" (Sanhedrin 93b). Maimonides read the animals as a parable of Israel living safely among once-hostile nations, and set 11:9 at the end of his Mishneh Torah as the goal of history: the whole world occupied with knowing the LORD. The ingathering of exiles in 11:12 is a petition of the daily Amidah.
views.X: The New Testament sees the Spirit resting on Jesus at his baptism (Matthew 3:16; John 1:32–33), the root of Jesse who rules the nations (Romans 15:12), and the Root of David who has won (Revelation 5:5; Revelation 22:16). The Greek and Latin list of seven spirits became the church's "seven gifts of the Holy Spirit" (Catechism 1831). Many Christians read 11:6–9 of the new creation, and premillennial Christians of Christ's thousand-year reign.
views.F: Dispensational and premillennial readers take 11:6–9 and 11:11–16 literally: a restored Israel regathered to its land, and a renewed creation, under Christ's rule on earth before the final new heavens and earth. Jewish hope too places the regathering of 11:12 in the days of the Messiah.

deep.h: The Messiah of chapter 11 at Qumran and in the New Testament
deep.b:
By the 1st century BC chapter 11 was a central text for messianic hope. The Qumran commentary on Isaiah (4Q161) reads the shoot as "the Branch of David" who will rule the nations at the end of days. Another Qumran text (4Q285) quotes 10:34–11:1 and speaks of the Branch of David, the Prince of the Congregation, putting the enemy's leader to death. The Qumran blessing of the Prince of the Congregation (1QSb 5:24–26) asks that he strike the peoples "with the breath of your lips" and be given "the spirit of counsel and everlasting might". The Psalms of Solomon 17 prays for a son of David "to destroy the unlawful nations with the word of his mouth". 1 Enoch 49:3 says of the Chosen One: "In him lives the spirit of wisdom".

The New Testament stands within that reading: the Spirit rests on Jesus (John 1:32–33), the lawless one is done away with "by the breath of his mouth" (2 Thessalonians 2:8), and Christ strikes the nations with the sword from his mouth (Revelation 19:15). What differs is the claim that the shoot has already come.

deep.h: The wolf and the lamb: literal or figurative?
deep.b: Isaiah 11:6–9 has been read in three main ways. Literally, on a renewed earth: Irenaeus took it as the state of creation in the kingdom after the resurrection (Against Heresies 5.33.4), and dispensational writers such as John Walvoord place it in the millennium. As a picture of peace among peoples: Maimonides read the wolf and the leopard as the violent nations, now at peace with Israel (Laws of Kings 12:1), and many Christians read it of the gospel making enemies into brothers. As new creation: many read the lines with 65:17–25 and Romans 8:19–22 as the healing of creation at the end, without deciding the details. The poem's own focus is clear on any reading: the violence that marks the world since Genesis 9:2 is undone, and the reason is that "knowing the LORD will fill the earth" (11:9). 65:25 repeats the scene in shorter form.

echoes: 6:13; 9:6–7; 10:33–34; 1 Samuel 16:1–13; 2 Samuel 7:12–16; Jeremiah 23:5–6; Zechariah 3:8; Psalm 72:1–4; Psalm 2:9; Habakkuk 2:14; 65:25; Hosea 2:18; Exodus 14:21–22; 19:23; 35:8; 40:3; Matthew 2:23; Matthew 3:16; John 1:32–33; Romans 15:12; 2 Thessalonians 2:8; Revelation 5:5; Revelation 19:15; Revelation 22:16
links: Seven gifts of the Holy Spirit
Seven gifts of the Holy Spirit

settings.what: The shoot of Jesse and the peaceable kingdom
settings.to: Judah, after the failure of its kings; later, a people with no king at all
settings.when: Hezekiah's reign or after the fall of David's dynasty
settings.why: After chapters of weak and faithless rulers, the poem draws the king God will give: filled with the Spirit, just to the poor, armed only with his word. His rule heals creation. For hearers who had seen Ahaz fail and the dynasty shrink to a stump, it promised that God's commitment to David's line had not died.
views: The poem comes from Isaiah, contrasting the true king with Ahaz (many conservative and some critical scholars).
The stump means the dynasty had ended in 586 BC; the poem is a later hope (many critics).

settings.what: The root of Jesse and the second exodus
settings.by: Isaiah, or a later prophet in his tradition
settings.to: Israelites and Judeans scattered across the known world
settings.when: After the Assyrian deportations; many date it after the Babylonian exile
settings.why: The oracle promises the scattered a new exodus: the king will be a rallying flag, the LORD will bring his people home from every direction, the old north–south feud will end, and a highway will run from Assyria as once from Egypt. For exiles it turned the memory of the exodus into hope for their own return.
settings.readers: The passage prepares for chapter 12, the song the returning people will sing, and for the highway and new exodus of chapters 35 and 40.

traditions.q: Does Isaiah 11:2–3 teach seven gifts of the Holy Spirit given to believers?
views: Yes. The seven gifts named in the Greek and Latin of Isaiah 11:2–3 (wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety and fear of the Lord) belong in their fullness to Christ and are given to the faithful, sustaining the moral life; they are given in baptism (Catechism 1266) and increased in confirmation (Catechism 1303).

The 1662 confirmation prayer asks God to "daily increase" in the candidates his "manifold gifts of grace", naming them from Isaiah 11:2–3: wisdom and understanding, counsel and ghostly strength, knowledge and true godliness, and "the spirit of thy holy fear".

The prayer at baptism in the Lutheran Book of Worship asks God to pour out on the newly baptized the spirit of wisdom and understanding, counsel and might, knowledge and the fear of the Lord, and joy in his presence. It follows the Hebrew list rather than a fixed doctrine of seven gifts.
The verse describes first the Spirit given without measure to Christ, from whose fullness believers receive. Reformed teaching follows the Hebrew and does not make a fixed list of seven gifts.
The gifts of the Spirit for believers are above all those of 1 Corinthians 12:8–10, received with the baptism in the Holy Spirit, rather than a list drawn from Isaiah 11:2–3.

traditions.q: When will the wolf live with the lamb (11:6–9)?
views: Literally, in the thousand-year reign of Christ on earth after his return, when Israel is restored to its land and the curse on nature is lifted.

Many Reformed teachers are amillennial: the picture is fulfilled in part in Christ's present reign through the gospel and fully on the new earth after the final judgment, not in a separate earthly millennium.

Postmillennial Reformed teachers read 11:9 as a promise for history: before Christ returns, the gospel will win the nations and bring a long age of peace, so that knowing the LORD fills the earth (Jonathan Edwards, Charles Hodge, Loraine Boettner).

Historic premillennialists hold that Christ returns before a thousand-year reign on earth, without the dispensational distinction between Israel and the church; the peace of 11:6–9 belongs to that reign and to the new creation after it (George Eldon Ladd).
The Church rejects millenarianism, the idea of an earthly reign before the end (Catechism 676). The peace of 11:6–9 is the messianic kingdom begun in Christ, to be completed when he comes in glory.
The thousand years are spent by the saints in heaven while the earth lies desolate; afterwards God makes the earth new, and the peace of 11:6–9 belongs to that new earth.

title: Springs of Rescue
sum: The first part of Isaiah closes with a song for the day of return. The singer thanks the LORD and asks that his anger turn back and give way to comfort; then: "Look, God is my rescue; / I will trust and not be afraid" (12:2), with words from the Song of the Sea. The people will draw water with joy from the springs of rescue.

A second hymn calls them to give thanks, call on the LORD's name, make his deeds known among the peoples and sing to the whole earth. It ends with a call to Zion to shout for joy, because the Holy One of Israel is great among them.
readings: Read as the song of the second exodus
As Israel sang after crossing the sea (Exodus 15), the regathered people of 11:11–16 sing here. The song quotes Exodus 15:2 and ends with the LORD in Zion's midst.
Read as the close of chapters 1–12

The song answers the book's opening: a people rebuked by the Holy One of Israel (1:4) now praise him among them; the anger of the refrain (9:12–10:4) has turned; and the name of Isaiah, "the LORD saves", sounds in the word "rescue" three times.
Read in worship
The words have lived on in Jewish and Christian liturgy: in Havdalah at the end of the Sabbath, in the water-drawing joy of the Feast of Booths, and as a canticle in Christian morning prayer.

views.H: The song has no named occasion. Its themes of return and thanks fit the hope of the exiles or the community after the return, and also the Temple worship of Isaiah's own Jerusalem.
views.C: Most scholars date chapter 12 after the exile, as an editor's closing hymn for chapters 1–11, built from phrases in Exodus 15 and the Psalms (Psalm 105:1; Psalm 118:14). Others think it was composed to round off an earlier collection.
views.J: The joy of the water-drawing at the Feast of Booths (Mishnah Sukkah 5:1) has long been tied to 12:3, and 12:2–3 opens the Havdalah blessing that ends the Sabbath. The verse is sung to the Israeli folk dance Mayim Mayim.
views.X: Jesus' cry on the last day of the Feast of Booths, "If anyone is thirsty, he should come to me and drink" (John 7:37), is often read against the water rite and 12:3. The song is a canticle of morning prayer in the Roman Liturgy of the Hours and in Anglican prayer books ("The First Song of Isaiah").
views.F: Many read the song as the anthem of the age to come, sung by Israel and the nations when the Holy One dwells in Zion, as in Revelation 15:3, where the redeemed sing the song of Moses and of the Lamb.

settings.by: The people ("you will say"), first as one voice (12:1–2), then all together (12:3–6)
settings.to: The LORD, then one another and the nations
settings.when: "On that day": the day of return promised in 11:11–16
settings.why: The song gives the people the words they will sing, before the rescue happens. It teaches them to read their history as the exodus story again: anger turned to comfort, and God present in Zion. Its call to tell the nations shows that Israel's rescue is meant to make the LORD known to all the earth.
settings.readers: For the readers of the collected book, the song closes the first major section, chapters 1–12, and points ahead to the songs of the new exodus in chapters 40–55.
